title: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted
description: For Monticah Hawkins, a 31-year-old real-estate agent in Atlanta, MySpace wasn't just a website – it was a ritual. "You could be authentic on MySpace,
body: For Monticah Hawkins, a 31-year-old real-estate agent in Atlanta, MySpace wasn't just a website – it was a ritual. "You could be authentic on MySpace," she says. "Upload raw images, no filters. You could have snot coming out your nose and nobody would judge." MySpace, once the world's biggest social network, is flirting with a comeback. Its owners, brothers Tim and Chris Vanderhook, say they plan to relaunch the platform, though no date or product details have been announced. A spokesperson for Viant, which owns MySpace, says the company does not have any updates to share "at this time." But just the idea of a comeback has stirred nostalgia among people who remember the MySpace days of more than 20 years ago as a place where personal pages were messy, loud, and deeply individual. It has also caught the attention of creators like Melissa Kristin, a TikTok star with more than 900,000 followers, who grew up on MySpace and remembers it as a more personal digital space. "It was all very much your own little world, your own corner of the internet," Kristin says. That sense of autonomy shaped how she expresses herself online today, and she believes that a revived MySpace should avoid the algorithmic, pay-to-play dynamics that dominate modern platforms. "It would be best served for personal connection rather than performance," she says. "Just to recapture that high we felt as millennials when we got all the friend requests and comments. It helped us feel connected." MySpace launched in 2003 and quickly became a cultural hub, helping artists like Arctic Monkeys, Adele, and Nicki Minaj find early audiences. But its highly customised pages, auto-playing music, and busy layouts eventually became a liability. Facebook's cleaner, simpler design pulled users away, and MySpace struggled through redesigns and ownership changes before fading from mainstream use. Marketing experts say any comeback will depend on learning from that history. Dr Alexa Fox, a marketing professor at the University of Akron, says the platform was a "first mover" in social media, but one that became too complex for many users. She believes MySpace's original strengths – music, creativity, and personal expression – could still resonate, but only with more accessible design. "It could be more user-friendly, with less coding involved," she says.Alex Mills, a social media strategist who has led campaigns for Spotify and Adobe, says the very thing people are nostalgic for, a feed without algorithms, was also "the thing that killed it." "People still want a feed," Mills says. "They just want a better one than the ones optimising for rage bait." Kevin McClary, head of performance marketing at Gorilla 76, believes MySpace should not try to compete directly with Meta, TikTok, or X. "They can be successful and sustainable even as a niche platform," he says, arguing it should be rooted in 2000s culture. McClary says leaning into MySpace's music identity could be a smart move, from profile songs to 2000s-themed festivals and merchandise. He believes the audience could be broader than former users, with younger generations embracing the early-2000s aesthetics they never experienced firsthand. "You see younger generations now buying old point-and-shoot digital cameras, MP3 players, even film cameras," McClary says. "They clearly have an interest in the past." MySpace could meet users where that trend is growing by becoming a place rooted in a "specific time," he says. He noted that creators making 2000s-style content on other platforms are often at the "mercy" of algorithms. Fox agrees that differentiation is essential. "MySpace shouldn't hang their hat on features other platforms already dominate," Fox says, pointing to Reels and short-form videos. Popular formats can be added, she says, but they should not define the platform. She also sees an opportunity to offer a calmer experience. Today's feeds, she notes, are "algorithmic-driven AI, constantly in your face." A platform where users have more control, or simply feel less overwhelmed, could stand out in a crowded market. For fans like Hawkins and Kristin, the appeal is emotional as much as practical. Both say they would return if MySpace kept its original spirit. For now, its comeback exists mostly as a promise – a reminder of a time when social media felt a little less polished and a lot more personal. "Are you still gonna have that same feeling?" Hawkins says. "Are you still gonna feel like, 'oh my god, somebody loves me?'"

schema.headline: Raw images, no filters: Why MySpace fans want it back as relaunch hinted

title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
description: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: Why?A major drive
body: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: Why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy."In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took."If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues."With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs."The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week."The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

schema.headline: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?

title: Gianni Infantino: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president
description: Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino. The st
body: Fifa has strongly criticised what it calls a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and its president Gianni Infantino. The statement follows a Daily Telegraph report, external which claimed Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment by Uefa after he had an affair while he was its general secretary.A Fifa spokesperson told the Telegraph Infantino "strongly denies" the allegations and that they are "categorically untrue".Fifa has now itself hit out at "unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims", adding that "speculation and insinuation should not be presented as fact".Infantino has come under increasing pressure from Uefa and European football associations over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.Uefa has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) president Lise Klaveness on Friday called on the Swiss-Italian to resign.European football's governing body says its threat to boycott Fifa events remains on the table, adding that assurances the FFE plan could not be revived have not been received."The Fifa president was democratically elected by Fifa's Member Associations and continues to serve with their mandate," Fifa said in its statement on Saturday."It is increasingly evident that there is a concerted and ongoing effort by some to undermine Fifa and its president. "Those who do not have the support of Fifa's member associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through Fifa's established democratic processes."Opposition to Infantino is largely from within Europe.The Mexican Football Federation broke ranks with its regional governing body Concacaf to come out in support of Infantino.It echoed a statement from Conmebol - South America's governing body - in saying it would reject any attempt to remove Infantino without a vote involving all 211 Fifa member countries.Infantino is also unanimously backed by the 54 nations of the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Fifa criticises campaign to oust president

title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
description: Trump last month announced "a monumental step toward lasting peace and security" after Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza.But Neta
body: Trump last month announced "a monumental step toward lasting peace and security" after Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza.But Netanyahu said that Hamas had to disarm before Israel withdrew its forces from Gaza, adding it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament". He said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward."They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.Just months before Israeli elections, the Israeli prime minister is unlikely to want to make concessions. He has faced calls from his far-right allies to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".It signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.

schema.headline: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says

title: Burnham to set out cost-of-living measures as he tours UK
description: The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Down
body: The prime minister is set to announce "a series of measures to make life easier" for those struggling with the cost of living in the coming days, Downing Street says.No 10 says Andy Burnham's plans are to "give people some room to breathe". He will also focus on ways of "improving high streets" as he embarks on a tour of the UK.But the government is facing continued pressure over its early release scheme for prisoners in England and Wales – with criticism of the fact that two of PC Andrew Harper's killers will be eligible from next year.Burnham is also likely to face pressure for more action on the cost of living – although significant interventions are unlikely before October's Budget.Even then, Chancellor John Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" – which will limit how much the government has to spend.The prime minister has been on holiday this week, but Downing Street said he would be in "listening mode" in the coming days as he tours the UK's nations and regions and works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".A spokesman for the prime minister said: "He thinks Westminster has got used to telling people that everyday hassles – like hidden pricing and consumers being ripped off – must be accepted as part of life. "He doesn't think that's right. That's why he's going to start rolling out a series of pro-consumer cost of living measures to give people some room to breathe."The spokesman added: "He's also going to be kicking off his summer tour around the country, getting out of Westminster and meeting people where they are. "The prime minister is going to be in listening mode to help inform his 10-year plan to bring back hope and make Britain better off."There are, though, likely to be continued questions about the forthcoming early release scheme, due to start in October.One of Burnham's first acts in Downing Street was to order a review which limited the range of people who would be eligible.But those convicted of manslaughter will still qualify for the scheme – including two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper.The prime minister has faced calls from PC Harper's family, former senior police officers and opposition politicians for them to be denied early release.But he has said he cannot go any further without risking prison capacity. Downing Street said on Saturday night that position remained unchanged, despite reports the prime minister could revisit the case.Despite early release schemes having been in place for England and Wales since late 2023 under the previous Conservative government, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) has warned the prison population could overtake capacity as soon as this November.The latest figures for England and Wales, recorded on 23 August, showed the prison population was at 86,495 - more than 97% of useable capacity.On the cost of living plans, the Conservatives said the government's "tax hikes and red tape are hammering our high streets".Shadow chancellor Mel Stride said: "This is breathtaking hypocrisy from Burnham… they are forcing businesses to close, destroying jobs and driving up prices for the public. "Meanwhile, Labour are plotting to release dangerous criminals onto our streets, leaving people feeling unsafe in their communities."Liberal Democrat Treasury spokeswoman Daisy Cooper said struggling high street businesses "need more than a new PM embarking on a vanity tour this summer".She said the PM should adopt the Lib Dem plan for high streets: "That means reversing the damaging jobs tax, delivering an emergency VAT cut for hospitality, replacing broken business rates and cracking down on the ghost landlords leaving our shop fronts vacant."Reform UK's economic spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "If Andy Burnham wants to help people with the cost of living, he should scrap the green levies and taxes on energy bills and rule out tax rises at the Budget."

schema.headline: Burnham to set out cost-of-living measures as he tours UK

title: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching wea
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPhilippa RoxbyHealth reporterFlip-flops have always been a popular solution to sweaty, uncomfortable feet in scorching weather  - and now they've had a revamp. The most stylish way to wear them this summer is with a kitten heel, according to fashion expert and trend forecaster Angela Baidoo."It's not a high heel and it's really kind of easy to just slip in and slip out of," she says.However, heel or not, the flip-flop has earned itself a bad rap for lack of support and damaging our feet. Is that fair? Why your summer shoe could be bad for you"In terms of arch support and joint support, it's not the best style, but people are investing a bit more, getting their flip-flops customised, because it's something that is just so easy to wear," Baidoo says.Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite, who is also chief clinical adviser at the Royal College of Podiatry, says it's "not accurate" to say flip-flops are bad.The problem comes if you go straight from wearing a very structured shoe to wearing flip-flops a lot, she explains. It means your foot is under more strain than normal, which makes you more prone to injury."The foot does start to change shape and tends to splay a little bit over time," says Branthwaite."A good analogy is if you were to wear a corset all the time and then took the corset off, everything would sort of all hang out, so to speak."So what are the stylish and comfortable alternatives?How to find healthy sandalsBaidoo suggests a more supportive flip-flop, such as a FitFlop, which is sturdier and contoured - a world away from the flat and thin flip-flops that have been cut from a big sheet of foam.Sliders are out and Crocs are in for Gen Z, she says. They might be "anti-fashion shoes" but they're "really comfy" and designed "orthopaedically" with footbed sandals like Birkenstocks offering the same advantages.The wooden clog is also making a comeback. It's worn by doctors and chefs on their feet all day. Scholl slider mules are the original orthopaedic shoe, Baidoo says - and admits she once had a pair in pink suede.Wedges are another option in the heat. "When I speak to some of my friends and some of my clients who work in the plus-size category, the wedge actually provides a form of comfortable footwear. And it provides a nice kind of silhouette for the ankle. You've got the support all the way through the shoe."Image source, Getty ImagesYou could always opt for the fisherman-style sandal, which looks like something a history teacher might have worn in the 1970s. With socks."Men can wear it as an alternative to a loafer. It's not as casual as a flip-flop, which might not be suitable for certain environments. It's a really cool kind of style to adopt for women too," Baidoo says.So what about the trend for wearing minimalist barefoot shoes? It's all about easing into them, says Branthwaite. In other words, don't buy a pair and then decide to go on a 5-mile hike.Expert tips for happy feet Podiatrist Dr Helen Branthwaite's top tips for looking after your feet: Pay close attention to the sole of the shoe and what it's made from, because that will influence how your foot moves and how you walkIf you can bend your flip-flops in two, then ask yourself if you're strong enough to take on the extra load your normal shoe would supportDon't forget to check the condition of your feet - the skin can dry out quickly in open footwear like flip-flops. You might not notice until your heel gets firmer and your toenails start to look fragileLather your feet in emollient, a moisturising water retention cream containing urea to hydrate the skin, every dayYour feet change constantly throughout your life, so get them measured regularly. Just because you start out being a size 6, doesn't mean you'll remain a size 6.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: From flip flops to fisherman's sandals: How to look after your feet this summer

title: Why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many
description: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uni
body: On the night of 15 August 2019, Lissie Harper got a knock at the door. She thought it was her husband Andrew coming home from work.Instead, it was uniformed officers, there to tell her that the man she had married four weeks earlier had been killed while on police duty."Everything I had known in my life to be true was robbed away. Every ounce of beautiful peace, gone," Lissie later said of the moment she was told.They had met as teenagers and were together for 13 years.In her eulogy at his funeral, Lissie recalled how Andrew would pass her notes in class.They were, she said, "true childhood sweethearts, loving one another more and more with each passing day".They had been about to go on their honeymoon.But, on that night nearly seven years ago, everything changed.The case has been back in the headlines because two of PC Harper's killers – Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole – will become eligible to be released early under government plans to tackle prison overcrowding.As the disturbing details of the case are revisited, his family, fellow officers and the public are outraged once more – at what happened, and at the perpetrators' impending release.PC Harper's death was brutal and devastating, causing shock, anger and an outpouring of grief across the country.Pictures of the smiling faces of his teenage killers laughing and joking as they left court only added to that anger.PC Harper had been about to head home at the end of a long shift when he and a colleague were called to reports of a burglary.He was "going beyond the call of duty", the prosecutor at the Old Bailey trial in 2020 said.During the case, haunting dashcam footage from the police patrol car was played showing the moment PC Harper confronted teenagers Henry Long, Bowers and Cole down a dark country lane. He then disappeared from view.His ankles had got caught in a strap trailing behind the car being driven by Long that had been used to tow a stolen quad bike.PC Harper was dragged for over a mile. He died on the road. His police badge and stab vest were found scattered along the route.The three teenagers were tried for murder. In the end, the jury convicted Bowers and Cole of manslaughter. Long had already pleaded guilty to that offence.It meant the jury was not sure that PC Harper's killers knew they were dragging the officer behind the car.But the Judge, Mr Justice Edis, described it as a manslaughter case which was "very close to a case of murder" in its seriousness.Some 6,000 prisoners had been due to be let out early under a law aimed at making space in the prisons system.Burnham paused that policy for a review after a public backlash, with particular focus on the possible release of two of PC Harper's killers after serving half rather than two-thirds of their sentences.But on Monday, while it was confirmed that about 1,000 prisoners would be excluded from the scheme, Bowers and Cole were not among them.Lissie described this as "disgraceful and disgusting", while PC Harper's mother said she was "devastated".A petition against their release has received more than 750,000 signatures.Long, the driver, is not eligible for early release.Recent weeks have shown just how much the case continues to stir strong emotions.Tiffany Lynch, chair of the National Police Federation of England and Wales, said that for rank and file officers up and down the country it "feels personal" – "there is disgust, upset"."We have a police officer who was four weeks into his marriage, dedicated to his job, responding to an incident of burglary, that our public expect of our police, has sacrificed his life in the line of duty and the people are not fulfilling their sentence," she said. "It just doesn't make sense."Stuart Blaik, the senior investigating officer in PC Harper's case, told BBC Breakfast his killers' early release was "particularly hard to understand" and would impact police morale.Justice Secretary Alex Norris has apologised to victims and their families and said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".

schema.headline: Why PC Andrew Harper's story touched so many

title: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG
description: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second h
body: The sample size was only 26 minutes.Yet the little combinations between Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes after both were introduced in the second half of Manchester United's 1-1 draw with Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg drew an appreciative response from senior figures at the club.With much made of United's activity - or lack of - in the transfer market this summer, it was good timing that Tielemans could make his debut when Mason Mount, arguably the club's player of pre-season, needed to be replaced after just 20 minutes.Head coach Michael Carrick told Norwegian broadcaster VG post-match that Mount had come off as a precaution after taking a hefty blow to his foot. The former Chelsea midfielder walked freely past reporters to the team bus an hour after the final whistle.Nevertheless, Tielemans was a surprise signing when Manchester United triggered a previously unknown £35m clause in the Belgian's contract at Aston Villa to agree a five-year deal.There was a lot of debate in the immediate aftermath about how much football the 29-year-old, who made his professional debut for Anderlecht when he was just 16, had played.It obscured his talent.Against PSG he did not do anything particularly special.There were a couple of 45-yard cross-field passes that found their intended targets. There were some simple first-time lay-offs to team-mates within 10 yards.There was also a short sprint just outside the United area to close down dangerman Khvicha Kvaratskhelia when Tielemans recognised the PSG star could be about to take possession within shooting distance.He got there, won the ball and played a simple pass, taking the ball out of harm's way.This isn't really what got the United contingent purring.They were reacting to the little passes between Tielemans and Fernandes, which allowed United to ease their way out of trouble or move up the pitch.Fernandes was the key man last season as United finished third. Nine goals and 21 assists was a decisive contribution in returning the club to the Champions League after a two-year absence.Tielemans showed in his brief cameo he can take some of the pressure off the Portuguese."Youri has consistently been one of the most outstanding midfielders in the Premier League throughout the past seven years," said director of football Jason Wilcox on Tielemans' signing."He will add further composure, creativity and leadership to our squad."He has all of the technical qualities, as well as the ambition and mentality, to thrive at Manchester United."If Wilcox reflects on those words as United head off to the Republic of Ireland for their week-long training camp in Maynooth, he can be quite pleased with himself.It was only 26 minutes, but on that evidence, he has got it spot on.Carrick has confirmed Marcus Rashford will rejoin the Manchester United squad for their trip to the Republic of Ireland.Rashford, England team-mate Kobbie Mainoo and Argentina defender Lisandro Martinez are the final three players to return for United after the World Cup.Although it was not expected Rashford would return to the club when he joined Barcelona on loan in July 2025, the La Liga champions failed to trigger a £26m option to buy the 28-year-old at the end of the season.Despite interest elsewhere, there has been no deal, meaning Rashford will return to United for the first time since January 2025, when he moved to Aston Villa after falling out with former manager Ruben Amorim.United are training at the plush Carton House hotel in Maynooth and have a friendly with Leeds United at Croke Park on 12 August.They complete their pre-season programme against Amorim's new club AC Milan in Wroclaw on 15 August, when Rashford could make his first United appearance since December 2024 if Carrick decides Wednesday is too soon.A former team-mate, coach and manager of Rashford, it has been felt if anyone can patch up the relationship between club and player - which includes his number 10 shirt being given to Matheus Cunha who is also due to be on the trip after a minor injury ruled him out of the Gothenburg encounter - it is Carrick."I've played with him. I played in the game he made his debut, so we have a history," Carrick said."We have got a full squad this week in Dublin. We fly straight there and have a few days where we have the whole group back together. Marcus is part of that, and Kobbie [Mainoo] and Lisandro [Martinez]. We look forward to seeing them."

schema.headline: Youri Tielemans: Man Utd midfielder impresses on debut against PSG

title: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing
description: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She
body: Clementine Wade, an education consultant and content creator, says there are things students can do to prepare for clearing ahead of results day. She suggests writing down all possible outcomes that you could get, and then finding alternatives to those outcomes. For example, depending on available places:If I get AAA, then I could do physics at SussexBBC could be physics at AberystwythCCD could be physics at Nottingham TrentThe Ucas website has a search tool to find courses, which you can find here, external. You can filter the options to the year of study, type of course and to those with clearing vacancies. It is the only official vacancy list, so it is the most up-to-date.For those who are unsure about their course choice and want to change, Wade says it is important to talk to a trusted adviser first, like a family member or teacher. She says students should think about why they chose that option in the first place, and why you might now be changing your mind.She says she finds most of the people who go through clearing are those that are applying to university for the first time.Haadi Nasir, a student at the University of Manchester, was one of those people. At first, he wanted to take a gap year after his A-levels so did not apply for university, but was persuaded to go by family and friends after achieving "great grades". On the day, with the help of his A-level teachers, he filled in a Ucas form, applied to six universities via clearing and picked the University of Manchester to study politics and modern history. "The good thing about clearing is that you can apply to as many universities as you want, unlike with Ucas, where you are limited to five," he says."That was definitely stress-relieving," he says.For those on the fence about university, Nasir recommends people put in a Ucas application "just in case" to avoid the stress of results day. That's a piece of advice that is echoed by Wade."You will need a referee, which is why I'd suggest doing it now," she says."Let's say [you've] got to email the teacher, the teacher's got to add a reference, then Ucas only gets sent once all of those parts are sent together."Nasir says he wished he was more prepared for clearing, and advises students to write down some notes on location, accommodation and cost for each university you contact. "Make sure you know whether you qualify before calling," he says."With my university I was required to have a specific A-level, so make sure you meet the requirements."Ucas updates at 08:00 on results day, so you can often find out whether you have been accepted to your firm choice before knowing your results. But Wade advises holding off and waiting until you get your results before you open the Ucas website. "I would say try and steer away from the temptation, get your results in hand and then look at your Ucas track, because then you can action that decision as opposed to having 90 minutes of freak-out."Jamie Bradford, head of future students at Leicester De Montfort University, also says it is easier to start conversations about clearing with your results in hand. On Ucas, before you add a clearing choice in your application, you need to contact the university or college and give them your clearing number - which you can find in your application - and personal ID, so they can find it."It's amazing how many students don't actually talk about the course or the place at all," says Bradford. "All they want is just the offer - 'I've got these grades, can you take me?' - in reality, it's three or more years of your life. The university is a big decision."Bradford says students need to ask about the day-to-day of the course, the campus and whether accommodation is available. "Work up a priority list," he says."For us, it's about fitting the right student to the right course, not just about getting any offer."Wade says students should go through a list of alternatives, and once they have received offers and discussed student finance with the universities, have a break to chat with a trusted person. She also stresses that students need to have the confidence to pick up the phone and call universities. "I know it feels scary, but you are the client, you do get to ask these questions," she says."You don't even need to ring this university to say, 'Can I get into this course, please?' You could say, 'Hey, what course could you offer me?' Because you know what, universities need these students."Some universities, like Leicester De Montfort, also operate clearing through WhatsApp as well as via phone.

schema.headline: What to do before results day to get the most out of university clearing

title: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world
description: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge
body: Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, Mark Griffiths drove from Cheshire to Spain for the eclipse, stopping in France to take picturesByGeorge SandemanOn Wednesday, parts of Europe will be plunged into daytime darkness as the moon passes in front of the sun, temporarily blocking its light and casting a shadow across the continent.For many of us, it will be a once-in-a-lifetime experience. But for some, following eclipses has become something of an addiction.Armed with two high-spec cameras, a specialist telescope and a drone, Mark Griffiths has spent two days driving from Cheshire to Galicia - one of the best places to view the eclipse - to record the event.It's a hobby that started six years ago, when he went to Shetland to see the northern lights - though the weather was so dreary he "didn't see anything".But it didn't put him off and he soon found he couldn't stop. He loved the thrill of witnessing and capturing the sky's most spectacular events.Image source, under_the_lightsImage caption, The view towards the sky from the hill in Galicia where Mark hopes to capture the total eclipseHe's since filmed the northern lights numerous times - he goes to Iceland once a month and leads tour groups there - and has photographed various auroras, eclipses and bioluminescence.But this is his first total solar eclipse."I kept wanting more," he says, and Europe's first total solar eclipse for more than 25 years is "like what the World Cup is to football" for enthusiasts like him."I'll be honest, it's like an addiction now," he tells me.I'm speaking to him the day after he's finished his marathon drive from England, across France and into Spain. He only paused to take photos of the night sky and rest for a few hours in Bordeaux. "I'm quite sleep deprived."The path of total eclipse begins at the tip of Siberia before curving round the Arctic Ocean and crossing parts of Greenland and Iceland.It then proceeds across a stretch of the northern Atlantic Ocean before reaching northern Spain and finishing in the Mediterranean. Other parts of Europe will see a partial eclipse.The total eclipse is only expected to last a couple of minutes for people who watch it, but that doesn't deter eclipse hunters from crossing continents to witness it.Samantha Phillips-Brown and her husband Gregory have flown to Iceland and hired a camper van so they can drive to a remote area to see it.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory Phillips-Brown flew from upstate New York to Iceland to see the eclipseThis will be the second solar eclipse they've witnessed.It was the awe-inspiring power of the first one they saw, near their home in upstate New York in 2023, that convinced them to travel for this one. They booked their flights and van more than a year ago."It was such a phenomenal experience to see the Sun start going dark and hear, suddenly, the birds stop chirping," recalls Samantha. "It's just a very strange experience."Gregory thinks of how Iceland's first settlers must have felt witnessing such a phenomena more than a millennium ago, a time of mythological rather than scientific explanation."They really didn't know what was happening, didn't know how long it was going to last... it must have been quite terrifying for them, in a way."They are spending the days before the eclipse driving round eastern parts of Iceland to go hiking and camping.Image source, Samantha Phillips-BrownImage caption, Samantha and Gregory booked their flights and camper van more than a year agoThe path of totality crosses the western part of Iceland and they hope to find a spot in the Westfjords peninsula to witness it.Although they've heard rumours of roads being closed to stop too many people overwhelming the area, so are keen to get there a couple of days before the spectacle.Samantha, who her husband describes as an "obsessive travel planner", is all over the Facebook groups and social media pages being used by eclipse hunters to share information and advice.She's expecting a good turnout given the number of eclipse glasses she's seen people with in Iceland. "They're really trying to prepare everybody," she says."What I expect, as we start inching westward, is we're going to see more and more of them."Andrew Wills is also going to an island to see the eclipse, albeit a much warmer one: Majorca.He's travelling with his wife and his dad, who is 90. Father and son witnessed Europe's last total solar eclipse together in 1999 while stood atop St Agnes Beacon in Cornwall.The landmark, believed by some to be a Bronze Age bowl barrow, offers panoramic views across the Cornish countryside and out to the Atlantic. It was a cloudy day, remembers Andrew."We didn't see the shadow rushing across the sea towards us, though we did see the dawn appearing and it getting closer very quickly," he says. "It was awe-inspiring."Image source, Andrew WillsImage caption, Andrew Wills is travelling to Majorca with his wife and 90-year-old father to see the eclipseHe has high hopes for a clearer day in Majorca where he has booked a villa near the town of Andraitx, located in the west of the island.Andrew has earmarked a spot nearby he hopes will give a good view across the sea. Their location in the path of totality means the eclipse will likely happen low on the horizon."We're going to take a couple of camping chairs with us, so Dad can sit if we can get there an hour or so before."The islands of Majorca and Menorca will be the last places on land to view the eclipse before the Sun sets and the shadow disappears.Eclipses have fascinated Andrew ever since he saw his first in St Agnes all those years ago."We live on a planet where we have this amazing coincidence. Where the Sun is 400 times bigger than the moon but the moon is 400 times closer."And so when the moon passes in front of the Sun and between Earth, it casts this perfect shadow."It made him appreciate the delicacy of life on our planet in the way astronomer Carl Sagan once did when speaking of the Pale Blue Dot photograph."We are tiny little specks in a huge vast area of nothingness," says Andrew. "We're amazingly lucky to be alive."

schema.headline: What it's like to chase solar eclipses around the world

title: Man makes 1,700-mile round journey to save rare phone box on Scottish island
description: A man has travelled from Cornwall to the Isle of Lewis to make 52 calls from a rural telephone box in order to keep it in service. William Arnold, who
body: A man has travelled from Cornwall to the Isle of Lewis to make 52 calls from a rural telephone box in order to keep it in service. William Arnold, who works as an artist and photographer, took the 1700-mile (2,735km) round trip to visit the rare phone box in Einacleit as part of a project to preserve phone lines in rural communities.Ofcom guidelines state a minimum of 52 calls have to be made from a phone box each year in order for it to remain operational. "The project is slightly ridiculous and comedic," said William. "But there is also a serious point about how we communicate with each other and how these phone boxes are often vital rural lifelines."The 43-year-old has been working to save phone boxes since 2022."It all started on the Isle of Lewis when I was working on a photographic project and I wanted to call my partner who was staying back at the house to say I was going to be back late," he said."My mobile phone battery was nearly dead and I came across this pristine looking phone box that had the old yellow British Telecom branding from the 1980s."There was a phone in there and I was really excited because I hadn't used a phone box for years. But when I picked up the receiver, the line was dead and I was so disappointed."The phone box in Einacleit - or Enaclete - appealed to him as what is believed to be the last remaining connected double-door telephone kiosk in the UK.It is understood to have been adapted locally to combat the strong winds and weather conditions on the Isle of Lewis, with a single door previously been seen as potentially dangerous. William said it was difficult to find out which phone boxes were still operational, so he often had to rely on local knowledge.A local Facebook page helped him work out whether his chosen phone box was connected and accessible.Before his arrival, the phone box had been repainted - with the doors painted closed  - and a sign said "emergency calls only". But William had about £36 worth of 50p and 20p coins, and managed to make his 52 calls to 52 different people."It wasn't just 20 second phone calls, some people phoned me back so I had a few longer conversations," he said."It took me just under two hours but the weather was rotten."There were 45mph winds which people could hear on the phone and it was hammering it down, so there was about an inch and a half of water at the bottom and my feet were cold by the end."He phoned people who chipped in to his Crowdfunder for the phone box project, as well as a few others to make up the numbers."It is really fun to go into a phone box on the chance you get someone phoning up who you have never met," he said. "But for isolated places where there is no signal, you can call out if there is an emergency."This winter in Cornwall we had 100mph winds, which knocked out the power and water to several towns and villages for several days."Some of the villages had no normal mobile phone coverage, so having no internet as well meant the phone box was the only way of contacting the outside the world."Last year BT reviewed 47 phone boxes in the Western Isles, with 42 eventually marked for removal.A spokesperson said about 9,000 public payphones remain operational in the UK - down from about 20,000 two years ago. "Maintaining and operating a large estate of payphones costs millions of pounds each year, an obstacle that prevents more investment in full fibre broadband and mobile networks – which our customers tell us they want," the spokesperson said.But William believes it is important to keep some phone boxes in working order for public safety.He said there have been various appeals to give phone boxes a listed status.But for now, he hopes he can persuade local people to make the 52 calls required to keep the phone box in service themselves.

schema.headline: Man makes 1,700-mile round journey to save rare phone box on Scottish island

title: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol
description: When Lisa Rees took her first dose of weight-loss medication in April, she hoped she would end up losing a few kilograms.What she did not expect, thou
body: When Lisa Rees took her first dose of weight-loss medication in April, she hoped she would end up losing a few kilograms.What she did not expect, though, was the side effect she has described as the drug's "best benefit": as well as eating less food, she has been drinking much less alcohol.Lisa used to drink two bottles of wine on a night out, but now, after she has had a couple of glasses, the 46-year-old from South Wales finds that she "just physically cannot drink another drop".There is a growing body of research into the link between weight-loss drugs and alcohol consumption.The drugs, with brands including Wegovy, Mounjaro and Ozempic, contain semaglutide or tirzepatide, which mimic a natural hormone called GLP-1. This suppresses appetite and keeps people feeling fuller for longer, helping them to lose weight.Early research suggests that because these drugs affect the reward response in the brain, they can reduce cravings for substances including alcohol and nicotine, says Dr Christian Hendershot of the University of South Carolina. He published a small-scale study, external in 2025 in which participants with alcohol use disorder craved alcohol less while taking Ozempic. Alcohol use disorder, sometimes referred to as alcoholism, is described by the NHS as drinking in a way that is harmful.A study, external from the University of Colorado Anschutz published last week also suggested that GLP-1 medications in pill form led to fewer days of heavy drinking in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder.People taking the drugs told BBC News that alcohol had affected them in different ways: some said their cravings for it had gone, drinking had made them feel nauseous or uncomfortably full, or they had got drunk more quickly. Others said they had not noticed any effect on their relationship with alcohol.Before she started taking Wegovy, Lisa says she drank between six and eight bottles of wine a week with friends. But she had sometimes worried about whether this was too much and whether it could damage her health.NHS guidance, external is that people should not drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis, which is about six medium glasses of wine or six pints. Drinking too much in the long term can lead to liver damage, high blood pressure and increased risk of cancer.Lisa says that since starting on the medication she has more than halved her consumption. At a recent day festival, she drank three glasses of wine over the course of nine hours. Previously, she would have had two bottles plus a couple of vodka mixers, she says.Alcohol has always been a big part of her social life and when she stopped drinking for a few weeks in the late 2010s, she realised friends had stopped inviting her to social events. It led her to start drinking again.This time round, Lisa says that she still looks forward to drinking wine, but after having a couple of glasses she simply cannot stomach any more."I still feel involved in things because I'm still drinking but drinking a lot less," Lisa says.For years, Warren Thomas, 45, from Colchester, had enjoyed an occasional beer with his family after work, as well as one or two heavy drinking sessions with his friends each month.But when he spoke to his friends on weight-loss medication about his plans to start taking Mounjaro, they warned him that it could affect how much he drank.Warren says he noticed the effect within 24 hours of his first dose in mid-June. "I just don't want to drink," he says. "I've just got no appetite for it."When he went out for his friend's birthday last month, he felt "light-headed and a little bit giddy" after two beers, he says."My tolerance level to drinking is now zero," he says.There is no formal advice in the British National Formulary, a guide to dispensing medicine used by doctors and pharmacists, about whether people on weight-loss drugs should  stop drinking alcohol, says Prof Russell Hearn, a GP and professor of medicine at King's College London.But he gives careful advice to his patients. "Alcohol has a lot of calories in it and if your goal is to lose weight, drinking less will definitely help you with that alongside changing your diet while you're on a GLP-1," he says.For people like Lisa and Warren, drinking less alcohol has been a happy bonus. But recent graduate Faye Goodwin, 20, feels that it has hampered her social life.When Faye drinks she says she gets nauseous very quickly and sometimes throws up or gets bad acid reflux.Faye, who got in touch with BBC Your Voice, has been taking Mounjaro since she was 18 and does not really know what it is like to drink alcohol without the impact of weight-loss medication. But she says she once took a month off the jabs and was able to drink without experiencing any nausea.At her age, alcohol is an important part of her social life, she says.Sometimes if she is due to go on a night out on injection day, she delays her jab by a day because she feels the impact of her medication on alcohol is the strongest in the day or two after she injects.She has occasionally turned down plans with friends if she has already taken her dose of medication that day. When she does drink, she usually consumes much less than everyone else. She feels this has affected her ability to form and maintain friendships, and made it hard for her at university in Cambridge when a lot of social events revolved around alcohol."It was difficult to enjoy it knowing I'd have to sit there sober while everyone else has a good time drinking, and oftentimes if I have tried to drink even a glass of wine or something I can't finish it because of the overwhelming nausea," she says.Observational studies of the general population suggest that people drink less overall when on weight-loss drugs, but the clinical trials to date have focused on people with alcohol use disorder, rather than occasional drinkers.Data is "accumulating very quickly", says Hendershot, adding that some facilities in the US are already prescribing the medication off-label to people with alcohol use disorder. Larger studies, with more participants and carried out over a longer period of time, are needed before it can be approved by regulators for the treatment of alcohol use disorder, says Dr Joseph Schacht, who carried out the study on weight-loss pills and alcohol.There are still unanswered questions around whether it is safe for people without obesity and diabetes to use the drugs for addiction treatment, and whether they will be affordable, says Dr Darren Quelch, who researches addiction at the University of South Wales.The drugs can also have a number of side effects, including rare but serious pancreatitis.Researchers are also looking into whether GLP-1 medications could be a treatment for other addictions, including smoking and opioids.Warren says starting on weight-loss jabs has put him off going out for drinking sessions with friends. "I don't really want to do it… I've just got no real desire for drinking."Though he never saw his drinking as problematic, it has still been a welcome change. "To cut it out completely has been very refreshing, without really trying," he says.

schema.headline: How weight-loss medication is changing relationships with alcohol

title: 'Minion Man' paints over obscene graffiti on Salford estate
description: Figure caption, Salford's 'Minion Man'  paints over anti-social graffitiByKaya Black and Lauren HirstNorth WestA street artist known as the "Minion Ma
body: Figure caption, Salford's 'Minion Man'  paints over anti-social graffitiByKaya Black and Lauren HirstNorth WestA street artist known as the "Minion Man" has turned his attention to brightening up his area's dirty and vandalised street cabinets.Martin Withers was given his new nickname after he painted bollards in Salford, Greater Manchester, to look like Minions from the Despicable Me films.Now the 38-year-old from Little Hulton has branched out to paint other popular cartoon characters - including from The Simpsons and Tom and Jerry - to cover up swear words."I'm just looking for something to clean the estate up," said Withers, who has lived in Little Hulton for more than 20 years.Image caption, Martin Withers said he was determined to clean up his local area with street artHe added: "Everyone puts a bad name on council estates but this is just something to give [back]."Withers said he decided to take action after seeing swear words daubed on various street cabinets."Instead of swear words everywhere, it's a lot better."I like to give the kids something, so I've been trying to think of popular characters for children."The green cable boxes belong to BT Openreach.A spokesperson for the communications company said: "Our street cabinets already play an important role in keeping local communities connected – so it's always great to see them being used to bring people together in other ways like this."Image caption, Vintage cartoon characters are among those featuring in Withers' street artWithers has also added to the collection of Minions bollards by painting female versions of the characters.Withers, who was diagnosed with epilepsy in 2019 after experiencing symptoms since he was a teenager, said he had also created a "special one" one in tribute to the NHS which had helped him.Image caption, Withers initially turned bollards into Minions Withers said he appreciated the kind words from those who had seen his work. "It has helped me get out instead of just sitting there... and gives me something to do," he said. "It makes me feel good."Sometimes I wonder why I'm doing it, but then people come up and say 'that's really nice that', and that's what makes my day."I didn't think so many people could know me."Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Greater Manchester

title: Huge wasp nest takes over Norfolk Wildlife Trust workers office
description: Image source, Eilish RothneyImage caption, Eilish Rothney said she first noticed the nest in June after being out conducting surveys on the reserves s
body: Image source, Eilish RothneyImage caption, Eilish Rothney said she first noticed the nest in June after being out conducting surveys on the reserves she managesByNeve Gordon-FarleighA nature reserve manager has been working from home after a group of wasps took over her office and built a 1m (3.2ft) nest around a bookshelf of ring binders.Eilish Rothney, a nature reserve manager for the Trinity Broads at the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, said after weeks of being out conducting surveys, she returned to her office on 11 June in Ormesby St Michael and saw wasps "buzzing round the corner". She found a nest about "a quarter of the size it is now" and said she worked for more than two hours before calling it a day. "It was just fascinating to watch the wasps coming and going and building up the lovely layers of colour — it looks like exotic paper," she said. Image source, Eilish RothneyImage caption, Wasps had taken over part of the office"It starts on the floor behind a box I put there, and they've come up on the inside and spread out on the box, and they've gone in all the little crevices around the binders and shelves."Image source, Elizabeth DarkImage caption, Eilish Rothney, who has been working from home, said the nest will be left until the autumn when the wasps will naturally leaveShe said wasps on the marshes would have to deal with roaming cattle and sheep, so she challenged her inner "ungulate" to stroll through the office like a "browsing cow".In the autumn, it is expected the wasps will leave the nest.She said: "The intention is just to leave it be and eventually they will all leave. The females who emerge will then go off and try and hibernate and come back next spring as queens. All the worker wasps will eventually die off and go hunting for food."Image source, Eilish RothneyImage caption, The nest had swamped parts of the office, binders and other itemsA picture of the nest was shared by the Norfolk Wildlife Trust, external, which said: "Thousands of new colleagues moved in without permission, skipped recruitment entirely and ignored the office hot-desking policy."While people have been divided in the post's comments, Rothney said people do not need to be afraid of them.She said: "I would encourage people, if you've got wasps that are bothering you, just to keep calm and try and move away. If you keep calm, they will sense that and won't feel threatened."Do you have a story suggestion for Norfolk? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice
